newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union to confront GM, Ford on outsourcing.
newsitem.headline: Canada union to confront GM, Ford on outsourcing.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union Tuesday vowed to extend its agreement with Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian subsidiary on limiting outsourcing when it confronts the Canadian units of General Motors Corp. and Ford Motor Col. at the bargaining table.

"Our history of bargaining in this industry is that once a pattern has been established, that becomes the pattern for the total industry," said CAW President Buzz Hargrove. "We'll deal with GM when we get to them."

Under the outsourcing agreement reached during tense bargaining Monday night between the CAW and Chrysler, the automaker cannot sell or close profitable plants or contract out the work without negotiating and replacing the lost work with other jobs.
Any restriction on outsourcing would have a big impact on GM, which has already announced plans to sell two plants in Ontario and contract out other work at a total cost of more than 5,500 jobs.
Auto analyst David Bradley of J.P Morgan Securities in New York said there is no way GM will accept such restrictions on outsourcing.
"GM will absolutely not agree to that, because they've already got two Canadian plants on the block," said Bradley.

But the union is equally adamant. "There can be no reduction of employment levels as a result of outsourcing," Hargrove told reporters during a break in bargaining Tuesday. "The important thing for us, is if the company is going to outsource work, they have to talk to us about the replacement work."
He said the contract language will include an embargo on selling or closing a workplace, or major part of a workplace, during the life of the three-year agreement.
GM Canada spokesman Stew Low acknowledged that outsourcing was important for GM, but he said he could not judge the impact of the deal reached with Chrysler until GM sees the contract language.
"We'll just have to work through that, see what has been agreed upon, see how that applies to our business, and respond at that point in time with the union," said Low.
Glynn Williams, an analyst at Newcrest Capital in Toronto, said the outsourcing pattern set by Chrysler will make it tough for GM and Ford to make a good deal with the union.

"It's going to make it harder for Ford and GM, GM especially, to cut the deal they would like to have from an outsourcing prospective," said Williams. "It was easier for Chrysler to give away than (it will be) for GM, who has a huge cost problem, and who has a huge requirement to outsource, much more than Chrysler does."

According to industry expert Dan Luria of Michigan's Industrial Technology Institute, Chrysler currently outsources about 66 percent of its work, more than either Ford, at about 62 percent, or GM, at 55 percent.

Chrysler and Ford contracted out much of their work over the past two decades during difficult financial times in order to cut costs. By contrast, all three automakers are now in a period of soaring profits. The union argues there is no way outsourcing can be justified.
GM, however, is anxious to shed its reputation as one of the highest-cost automakers in North America and would like to contract out more work to cheaper suppliers.
Newcrest Capital's Williams said the looming battle between GM and the CAW is too close to call. "GM is a powerful corporation, and the union is as well, so who knows," he said.
Hargrove already has sounded a warning that he is not optimistic a deal can be reached with GM without a strike.
